cards.title: The ACID Acronym
cards.teaser: ACID — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — is the foundational promise of a transactional database. But every word in the acronym is slippery, and every database interprets it differently.

runs.text: ACID was coined by Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter in 1983 to describe the properties that a database transaction must provide to be safe. The acronym is widely cited and poorly understood: each property has been diluted, reinterpreted, or violated by systems that still claim to be ACID.

items.text: Atomicity

— a transaction's writes either all succeed or all fail as a unit. If a crash occurs partway through, the partial writes are rolled back. Crucially, atomicity is about fault tolerance, not concurrency. It says nothing about what other transactions see while the transaction is in progress. The better term might be
abortability
: if anything goes wrong, you can safely abort and retry.
Consistency

— the most overloaded word in distributed systems. In the ACID sense, consistency means that application-defined invariants (e.g., "account balances must not go negative") must be preserved across a transaction. But this is the
application's
responsibility, not the database's. The database can only enforce constraints you declare (NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY). The C in ACID is therefore a property of the application, not the storage engine.
Isolation

— concurrently executing transactions are isolated from each other. The textbook definition is serializability: the outcome is equivalent to running the transactions one at a time, in some serial order. In practice, most databases default to something weaker — read committed or snapshot isolation — because full serializability is expensive.
Durability

— once a transaction commits, its data will survive any subsequent hardware fault, power loss, or crash. In a single-node database, this means writing to disk before acknowledging the commit. In a replicated database, it means persisting to multiple nodes. Perfect durability is impossible — if every disk in a data center simultaneously fails, data is lost. Durability is always a matter of degree.

runs.text: The C in ACID exists mainly to complete the acronym. Kleppmann's assessment: "The C in ACID is essentially a property of the application, not of the database... The database cannot check all possible invariants on your behalf." Don't rely on the storage engine to enforce business rules that only your application understands.

ACID is the classic safety promise for transactions. Atomicity means all-or-nothing; Consistency is a misleading term that really means your app's invariants hold; Isolation means concurrent transactions don't interfere; Durability means committed data survives crashes. The catch: databases often provide weaker versions than the textbook definitions.

cards.title: BASE — Basically Available, Soft State, Eventual Consistency
cards.teaser: BASE was coined as a marketing counterpoint to ACID — a way to describe NoSQL systems that deliberately relaxed transactional guarantees in exchange for availability and partition tolerance. It is less a rigorous definition than a declaration of priorities.

runs.text: BASE was introduced by Eric Brewer around 2000, building on the CAP theorem he had formulated the same year. It describes a different design philosophy from ACID:

items.text: Basically Available
— the system appears available most of the time. It may return stale, incomplete, or approximated data rather than returning an error. The system prefers a degraded response over no response.
Soft State

— the state of the system may change over time, even without new inputs, as replicas converge. Data is not guaranteed to be consistent at any given moment: nodes may hold different versions, and the state is considered "in flight" during convergence.
Eventually Consistent

— given no new writes and enough time, all replicas will converge to the same value. Eventual consistency does not specify how long convergence takes, nor does it say anything about which value will "win" — that depends on the conflict resolution strategy (last-write-wins, merge functions, CRDTs).

runs.text: ACID and BASE are not a binary choice. The framing is mostly historical: it arose in the early 2000s as NoSQL databases rejected the perceived overhead of relational transactions. In practice, many modern distributed databases provide tunable consistency — you can pick point-in-time consistency at the cost of latency, or eventual consistency for lower latency. Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak, and Couchbase occupy this space. Spanner and CockroachDB show that ACID is achievable at global scale.

Kleppmann is direct about BASE: "I think it is mostly a marketing term." The real tradeoffs are about which anomalies you are willing to tolerate — dirty reads, lost updates, write skew — not a choice between two vague philosophies. Understanding the specific anomaly model is far more useful than arguing ACID vs BASE.

BASE is the relaxed alternative to ACID: your data might be stale, replicas might temporarily disagree, but the system stays available and eventually converges. It is more of a design philosophy than a precise spec — the real question is always which specific consistency anomalies you are willing to accept.

cards.title: Single-Object vs Multi-Object Transactions
cards.teaser: Atomicity within a single row or document is almost universal — even a key-value store guarantees that a single write either lands or doesn't. The hard problems begin when a transaction must span multiple objects, or multiple rows in the same table.

runs.text: It is useful to separate two categories of atomicity, because databases handle them very differently:

items.text: Single-object atomicity

— guarantees that a write to a single object is atomic. If you increment a counter, the server either applies the increment or doesn't — you never observe a half-written value. This is provided by virtually every database, including key-value stores like Redis and DynamoDB. It is implemented with write-ahead logs and crash recovery, not with traditional transaction machinery.
Multi-object atomicity

— guarantees that writes to multiple objects (rows, documents, or tables) either all commit or all abort together. This is what people mean by "ACID transactions" in practice. Example: transferring money requires debiting one account and crediting another in a single atomic operation — neither can succeed without the other.

runs.text: Why multi-object transactions are necessary:

items.text: Foreign key references
— inserting a row that references another row must be atomic. Otherwise a reader can observe a dangling reference.
Denormalized data
— if a user profile is stored in two documents for performance, updating both must be atomic. A crash between the two writes leaves the data inconsistent.
Secondary index maintenance
— every indexed column is a secondary object. If updating the main row and its index are not atomic, a reader using the index can find a row whose values don't match the index entry.

runs.text: Many NoSQL databases historically avoided multi-object transactions because they are hard to implement efficiently across shards. MongoDB only added multi-document ACID transactions in version 4.0 (2018). FoundationDB, Spanner, and CockroachDB were designed from the start with distributed multi-object transactions.

Single-object atomicity — making sure one write lands cleanly — is trivial and universal. Multi-object atomicity — making sure a group of writes to different rows or documents all land together or all fail — is the hard part, and the real value of full ACID transactions.

cards.title: Dirty Reads
cards.teaser: A dirty read occurs when a transaction reads data that a concurrent transaction has written but not yet committed. If the writer aborts, the reader has seen data that, according to the database, never existed.

runs.text: Consider a transaction that writes two rows as part of a multi-object update. Another transaction reads the first row after it is written but before the second row is written — and before the first transaction commits. This is a dirty read: the reader sees a partially-applied state.

explanation.text:
-- Transaction 1 (T1): transfer $100 from Alice to Bob
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'alice';  -- written, not committed
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'bob';    -- not yet written
-- [T1 not yet committed]

-- Transaction 2 (T2): reads Alice's balance concurrently
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'alice';
-- T2 sees Alice's balance decreased by $100 (dirty read)
-- If T1 aborts, this balance never actually existed

runs.text: Dirty reads cause two categories of problems:

items.text: Reading rolled-back data

— if T1 aborts after T2 has read its uncommitted write, T2 has observed a value that was never durably committed. Any decision T2 made based on that value is predicated on data that "doesn't exist" from the database's perspective.
Partial multi-object writes

— as in the money-transfer example: a reader between T1's two writes sees Alice's account decremented but Bob's not yet incremented. The database is temporarily violating its own invariant, and a dirty-read transaction can observe that violation.

runs.text: The
read committed

isolation level (covered next) prevents dirty reads. Most production databases default to read committed or stronger, so dirty reads are rare in practice — but they are possible at the weakest isolation level (read uncommitted), which exists in MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server but is almost never the right choice.

A dirty read is seeing another transaction's work-in-progress — data it wrote but hasn't committed yet. If that transaction aborts, you've read data that never actually existed. It's like seeing a draft document that the author later deletes.

cards.title: Dirty Writes
cards.teaser: A dirty write occurs when a transaction overwrites data that a concurrent transaction has written but not yet committed. Unlike dirty reads, dirty writes can corrupt data in ways that violate application invariants even when both transactions individually succeed.

runs.text: Consider two buyers (T1 and T2) simultaneously purchasing the last item in a shop. Both transactions involve two writes: update the listing to mark it "sold" and insert a purchase invoice. Without protection from dirty writes:

explanation.text:
-- T1 and T2 both trying to buy the same car

-- T1 writes:
UPDATE listings SET buyer = 'Alice' WHERE id = 42;  -- T1 writes
-- T2 overwrites before T1 commits:
UPDATE listings SET buyer = 'Bob'   WHERE id = 42;  -- dirty write

-- T1 writes its invoice:
INSERT INTO invoices (listing_id, buyer) VALUES (42, 'Alice');
-- T2 writes its invoice:
INSERT INTO invoices (listing_id, buyer) VALUES (42, 'Bob');

-- Result: listing says sold to Bob, invoice says sold to Alice
-- The data is internally inconsistent

runs.text: The result is that the two tables are in disagreement: the listing says one buyer, the invoice says another. Both transactions "committed," but the combination is inconsistent because T2's write to the listing overwrote T1's uncommitted value, while T1's invoice write proceeded independently.

Read committed isolation (and all stronger levels) prevents dirty writes by delaying a transaction's write until the prior writer either commits or aborts. This is typically implemented by acquiring a row-level lock on write and holding it until commit.

Dirty writes are prevented by read committed isolation, but read committed does not prevent all multi-object anomalies. The lost-update problem — where two transactions each do a read-modify-write cycle and one overwrites the other's work — is still possible at read committed. That requires explicit locking or atomic operations to prevent.

A dirty write is when you overwrite another transaction's not-yet-committed write. Unlike dirty reads, dirty writes can corrupt your data even when both transactions succeed — the two halves of their multi-object writes get interleaved in inconsistent combinations.

cards.title: Read Committed
cards.teaser: Read committed is the default isolation level in Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and MemSQL. It makes two simple guarantees: you only read committed data, and you only overwrite committed data. Everything stronger costs more; this is the floor.

runs.text: Read committed provides exactly two guarantees:

items.text: No dirty reads
— when reading from the database, you only see data that has been committed. You never see a value written by a transaction that has not yet committed or has subsequently aborted.
No dirty writes
— when writing to the database, you only overwrite data that has been committed. The database delays your write if another transaction has an uncommitted write on the same row.

runs.text: Implementation: dirty writes are prevented by acquiring a row-level write lock for the duration of the transaction. Dirty reads are prevented
without

requiring readers to take a lock — instead, the database remembers both the old committed value and the new uncommitted value, and serves the old value to concurrent readers until the writing transaction commits. This avoids the "reader blocks writer" problem that plagued older locking-based approaches.
What read committed does NOT prevent:

items.text: Non-repeatable reads (read skew)

— if you read a value twice in the same transaction, you may see different results if another transaction committed between your two reads. This is acceptable for many workloads but breaks backups, analytics, and long-running read transactions.
Lost updates
— two transactions doing read-modify-write concurrently can overwrite each other's work.
Write skew and phantom reads
— covered in later cards.

runs.text: MySQL uses read committed as the default for non-transactional tables, and "repeatable read" (which MySQL implements as snapshot isolation) as the InnoDB default. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server default to read committed for InnoDB-equivalent engines. If your application requires stronger guarantees, you must request a higher isolation level explicitly.

Read committed is the most common default: you only see committed data and only overwrite committed data. It prevents the worst corruptions but still lets through subtler bugs like read skew and lost updates — for those, you need snapshot isolation or higher.

cards.title: Snapshot Isolation and Repeatable Read
cards.teaser: Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot of the database as it existed at the moment the transaction began. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers — the most powerful practical isolation improvement in database history.

runs.text: The canonical motivation for snapshot isolation is a backup or analytics query that runs for several minutes. At read committed, such a query can observe inconsistencies: early in its scan, it reads Account A's old balance; later, a concurrent transaction transfers money and commits; still later, the backup query reads Account B's new balance. The backup has seen a state that never actually existed at any point in time — money appearing to exist in both accounts simultaneously.
Snapshot isolation solves this by assigning each transaction a
snapshot timestamp

at the start, and ensuring it only sees data committed before that timestamp. The transaction gets a consistent, frozen view of the world — no matter how long it runs, it will never observe writes made by transactions that started after it did.

This implementation is called MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control — and is covered in detail in the next card. The important behavioral point is that snapshot isolation eliminates read skew (non-repeatable reads): reading the same row twice within a transaction always returns the same value, because both reads are served from the same snapshot.

A naming note: the SQL standard does not define snapshot isolation. Instead, it defines four isolation levels (read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable). MySQL InnoDB calls its snapshot isolation implementation "repeatable read," which is technically a superset of the SQL standard's repeatable read. PostgreSQL calls its implementation "repeatable read" as well. Oracle uses the term "serializable" for what is really snapshot isolation. This naming chaos is important: always check what a specific database actually provides, not just what it calls itself.

Snapshot isolation prevents: dirty reads, dirty writes, non-repeatable reads (read skew). It does NOT prevent: lost updates (in some implementations), write skew, or phantom reads (depending on the database). Snapshot isolation is not serializable — two snapshot-isolated transactions can produce outcomes that no serial execution could produce.

Snapshot isolation takes a photograph of the database at the moment your transaction begins and shows you that photograph for the entire transaction's lifetime. Long-running reads never see partially-applied writes, and readers never block writers because everyone is looking at their own frozen copy of the data.

cards.title: MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control
cards.teaser: MVCC is the mechanism that makes snapshot isolation possible: instead of overwriting rows in place, the database keeps multiple versions of each row tagged with transaction timestamps. A transaction's read sees the version current as of its snapshot; old versions are eventually garbage-collected.

runs.text: PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation is the canonical reference. Every row has two hidden system columns:
xmin
(the transaction ID that created this version) and
xmax
(the transaction ID that deleted or updated this version, or null if still current). When a transaction updates a row, it doesn't overwrite it — it creates a new version with the new values and a new
xmin
, and marks the old version with
xmax
set to the updating transaction's ID.

explanation.text:
-- Conceptual view of PostgreSQL heap storage during MVCC:
-- (xmin, xmax, data) represent version visibility

-- Initial state:
-- (xmin=10, xmax=null, balance=500)   <- current version, visible to txns >= 10

-- After T2 (xid=20) updates balance to 400:
-- (xmin=10, xmax=20,   balance=500)   <- old version, visible to txns that started before T2 committed
-- (xmin=20, xmax=null, balance=400)   <- new version, visible to txns that started after T2 committed

-- A read-only transaction that started at xid=15 (before T2)
-- will read balance=500 even after T2 commits

runs.text: Visibility rules: a transaction with snapshot timestamp T sees a row version if its
xmin
is committed and <= T, and its
xmax
is either null, or is a transaction that had not committed as of T. This is evaluated per-row on every read — no locks required.
The trade-off is storage bloat. Old row versions accumulate on disk until they are no longer needed by any active transaction. PostgreSQL's
autovacuum

process periodically scans tables and removes versions that are older than the oldest active transaction's snapshot (the "xmin horizon"). If long-running transactions prevent autovacuum from reclaiming space, tables can grow unboundedly — the "table bloat" problem that plagues write-heavy PostgreSQL deployments. MySQL InnoDB uses a similar mechanism with its purge thread to clean the undo log.

A single long-running transaction in PostgreSQL can prevent vacuum from removing any version created after it started. In a busy write-heavy database, this means dead row versions accumulate for the lifetime of that transaction. Always set statement_timeout or lock_timeout on long-running analytics queries to prevent accidental table bloat.

MVCC keeps old copies of every row rather than overwriting them. Each row version is stamped with the transaction that created it, and each reader's snapshot determines which version it sees. Old versions are cleaned up (vacuumed) once no active transaction needs them anymore.

cards.title: Lost Updates
cards.teaser: The lost update problem occurs when two transactions both read a value, compute a new value based on what they read, and write the result back — the second writer silently overwrites the first's work, as if the first transaction never happened.

runs.text: Lost updates arise in the read-modify-write cycle, one of the most common application patterns. Consider a page view counter:

explanation.text:
-- T1 and T2 both incrementing a counter concurrently

-- T1 reads:
SELECT views FROM pages WHERE id = 42;  -- T1 reads: 100
-- T2 reads:
SELECT views FROM pages WHERE id = 42;  -- T2 reads: 100 (same snapshot)

-- T1 writes:
UPDATE pages SET views = 101 WHERE id = 42;  -- T1 commits
-- T2 writes:
UPDATE pages SET views = 101 WHERE id = 42;  -- T2 commits, overwrites T1

-- Result: 101, not 102. One increment was lost.

runs.text: This pattern appears everywhere: incrementing a counter, appending to a list, updating a balance, editing a wiki page, modifying a JSON document. Any operation that reads before writing is vulnerable.
Four strategies prevent lost updates, in roughly increasing order of pessimism:

items.text: Atomic write operations
— express the update as a single atomic operation that the database executes without interleaving:
UPDATE pages SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = 42
. The database serializes these at the storage engine level. This eliminates the read-modify-write cycle entirely. Redis's INCR command and MongoDB's $inc operator are the document-store equivalents.
Explicit locking
— read with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to lock the row, preventing any other transaction from reading or writing it until you commit:
Automatic detection

— PostgreSQL's repeatable read and serializable modes automatically detect lost updates and abort one of the conflicting transactions, forcing a retry. MySQL InnoDB's repeatable read does not detect lost updates automatically — a significant difference that is easy to miss.
Compare-and-set (CAS)
— only apply the write if the value has not changed since you read it (covered in the next card).

runs.text: The lost update is the classic race condition of databases: two transactions read, both compute an update based on what they saw, both write — the second write silently clobbers the first. The fix is either to express the update atomically, lock the row before reading it, or use compare-and-set to detect the conflict.

cards.title: Compare-and-Set and Atomic Write Operations
cards.teaser: Compare-and-set is the no-lock primitive for safe concurrent updates: write a new value only if the current value matches what you last read. If someone else changed it since your read, your write is rejected and you retry. Atomic operations go further — they eliminate the read-modify-write cycle entirely.

runs.text: Compare-and-set (CAS) — sometimes called optimistic concurrency control at the row level — allows an application to detect that a concurrent modification happened and react to it rather than silently overwriting the competing write:

explanation.text:
-- Compare-and-set: only update if the value hasn't changed since we read it
-- We read balance = 500 previously
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = 400
WHERE id = 'alice'
  AND balance = 500;   -- the "compare" part

-- If another transaction changed balance before we ran this,
-- the WHERE clause matches no rows (rows_affected = 0).
-- The application must check rows_affected and retry if 0.

runs.text: CAS works when the database provides a current-value read — i.e., the WHERE clause is evaluated against the latest committed value, not your snapshot. In snapshot isolation, the
WHERE balance = 500

predicate is evaluated at the time of the write against the current state, so CAS works correctly. However, if the condition is based on a snapshot read that pre-dates concurrent commits, the application must be careful to understand what "current" means in its database's isolation model.
Atomic write operations are even better than CAS when the transformation can be expressed as a single operation. Databases typically implement these as:

items.text: SQL expressions
UPDATE t SET x = x + 1 WHERE ...
— the database takes a write lock on the row, reads the current value, increments it, and writes back, all as a single atomic operation.
Redis INCR / INCRBY
— Redis's single-threaded command execution guarantees atomicity at the command level without any transaction overhead.
CRDTs

— Conflict-free Replicated Data Types define merge functions for specific data structures (counters, sets, maps) such that concurrent writes can always be combined without conflict. Riak and Redis use CRDTs for replicated state.

runs.text: CAS is the underlying primitive for optimistic concurrency control (OCC), which is the basis of Snapshot Isolation with Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI). The idea scales up: instead of comparing a single value at write time, SSI tracks all reads a transaction made and aborts if any of those values were concurrently modified — a generalized CAS over the entire read set.

Compare-and-set says: "I'll only apply my write if the value hasn't changed since I read it." Atomic write operations say: "I don't need to read at all — express the whole update in one step and let the database handle the coordination." Both eliminate the race window between your read and your write.

cards.title: Write Skew and Phantom Reads
cards.teaser: Write skew is a subtle anomaly that snapshot isolation cannot prevent: two transactions each read overlapping data, each check an invariant, each write to disjoint rows — but their combined effect violates the invariant both individually validated. It's a concurrency bug that produces no dirty reads, no lost updates, and no obvious errors.

runs.text: Kleppmann's canonical example: a hospital requires at least one doctor on call at all times. Alice and Bob are both on call. Both simultaneously decide to take the night off because they see "there are 2 doctors on call — I can leave."

This is write skew. Each transaction individually respects the invariant. Neither performs a dirty read or a lost update. Yet the combined outcome violates the invariant that both were checking. The reason snapshot isolation cannot prevent this: Alice and Bob each read rows they do not themselves write to, so there is no write-write conflict for the database to detect.
Write skew generalizes to a pattern: a transaction reads some rows, makes a decision based on the result, writes to rows that are
different from the ones it read
. Other examples:

items.text: Meeting room booking

— two users check whether a room is free at 2pm (it is), then both book it. Each transaction reads the booking table and inserts a new row for a different time slot or user, so there is no lost update — but the room ends up double-booked.
Username registration
— two users check whether a username is taken (it isn't), then both insert rows claiming it. If each inserts a different row id but the same username, uniqueness may not be enforced.
Financial limits

— a user with $200 credit issues two $150 withdrawals simultaneously. Both read the balance as $200 and determine it is sufficient, then both write withdrawal records. The combined effect is a $100 overdraft.

runs.text: A
phantom read

is the specific flavor of write skew where the write inserts a new row that would have matched the original read's WHERE clause. In the meeting room example, the second booking inserts a row for the same room and time — a row that didn't exist when the first transaction did its availability check. Even if the first transaction re-read the booking table, it would now see a different result. Preventing phantoms requires either serializable isolation or materializing the conflict.

Write skew is the sneakiest isolation anomaly: both transactions check an invariant, both see it satisfied, both write to different rows — and together they violate it. No dirty reads, no lost updates, just two well-intentioned transactions whose combination breaks a rule neither individually violated.

cards.title: Materialising Conflicts and Predicate Locks
cards.teaser: When write skew arises because two transactions write to rows that don't yet exist, there is no object to put a lock on. Materialising conflicts creates the phantom rows in advance — turning a lock-less phantom into a lockable object. Predicate locks take the opposite approach: lock the predicate itself.

runs.text: The meeting room double-booking problem is a phantom: both transactions check for rows matching a predicate ("is this room free at 2pm?"), find none, and insert new booking rows. The conflict is between a read predicate and a subsequent insert — the inserted row would have satisfied the predicate had it existed at read time.
Two approaches to prevent phantoms without full serializability:

items.text: Materialising conflicts

— pre-populate the table with all possible "slots" so that the phantom becomes a real row that can be locked. For meeting rooms: create a row for every room/time combination in advance. Now checking availability means reading (and locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE) an existing row, not checking for the absence of rows. The conflict is materialized as a lock contention on the slot row. This is an artificial table created purely to carry locks, and it is usually considered a last resort — it leaks implementation detail into the schema.
Predicate locks

— instead of locking specific rows, lock the predicate: "lock all rows that would satisfy WHERE room = 'Narnia' AND time = '2pm' AND date = '2026-06-01'". Any transaction that inserts or updates a row matching this predicate must wait. InnoDB calls these "gap locks" — they lock the gap in a B-tree index between existing values where a new value could be inserted. PostgreSQL uses predicate locks in its serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) mode.

runs.text: Predicate locks are expensive if many transactions are checking the same predicate simultaneously — each must check whether its inserts conflict with any active predicate lock. 2PL implementations typically trade precision for performance by upgrading predicate locks to
table-level index range locks
when the predicate is complex, at the cost of false positives (blocking transactions that didn't actually conflict).

You can't put a lock on a row that doesn't exist yet — that's the phantom problem. Materialising conflicts pre-creates the rows so there's something to lock. Predicate locks take a different route: lock the search condition itself, so any future insert matching it must wait.

cards.title: Serialisable: Actual Serial Execution
cards.teaser: The simplest way to achieve serializable isolation is to execute transactions one at a time, in a single thread. VoltDB, Redis, and FoundationDB all use this approach. What sounds like a terrible idea turns out to be competitive with multi-threaded approaches when transactions are short and data fits in RAM.

runs.text: Actual serial execution was dismissed as impractical for decades: how can a single-threaded database keep up with concurrent workloads? The insight that made it viable came around 2007-2012, from two observations:

items.text: RAM is large enough to hold the entire dataset

— in-memory databases like VoltDB, Redis, and Datomic avoid the disk I/O bottleneck that made serialization slow on earlier hardware. A transaction that touches only cached data is measured in microseconds, not milliseconds.
OLTP transactions are short

— interactive transactions that wait for user input (the classic textbook transaction where a human decides something mid-transaction) are eliminated by requiring all reads and writes to be pre-declared. The database executes the entire transaction as a stored procedure, never waiting for network round-trips.

runs.text: VoltDB requires that all transactions be written as stored procedures in Java or SQL. FoundationDB uses a similar model: transactions are short, pure-compute, and express all their reads and writes before execution. Redis uses single-threaded execution for all commands and MULTI/EXEC for transaction blocks.
The limitations of actual serial execution:

items.text: Throughput limited to one CPU core

— the single-threaded bottleneck caps write throughput. VoltDB and FoundationDB scale horizontally by partitioning data across multiple single-threaded cores; cross-partition transactions require coordination and become slower.
No long-running transactions

— an analytics query that scans millions of rows would block the entire database. OLAP workloads are typically served from a read replica or a separate analytics system, not through the serial execution engine.
No interactive transactions
— the "read something, display it to the user, wait for their response, then write" pattern is incompatible. All reads and writes must be expressed upfront in the stored procedure.

runs.text: Actual serial execution is the approach chosen by FoundationDB (the storage engine underlying Apple iCloud and Snowflake's metadata store). Its simplicity provides correctness guarantees that are trivial to reason about — serial execution is the definition of serializability, not an approximation of it.

If you run one transaction at a time, you trivially have serializable isolation — no concurrency means no concurrency bugs. VoltDB and Redis do exactly this. It works when transactions are short, data is in memory, and you can partition across many single-threaded workers.

cards.title: Serialisable: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
cards.teaser: Two-Phase Locking is the classic locking-based approach to serializability: readers block writers, writers block readers, and all locks are held until the transaction commits. It provides true serializability but at the cost of high lock contention and latency.

runs.text: 2PL is named for its two phases: the
growing phase
(acquiring locks) and the
shrinking phase

(releasing locks after commit or abort). The key rule: once a transaction releases a lock, it may not acquire any new locks. This ordering guarantee is what provides serializability — it prevents the cyclic dependencies that would allow non-serial outcomes.
2PL uses two lock modes:

items.text: Shared lock (S lock / read lock)

— a transaction reading a row acquires a shared lock. Multiple transactions may hold shared locks on the same row simultaneously. A transaction wanting to write must wait for all shared locks to be released.
Exclusive lock (X lock / write lock)

— a transaction writing a row acquires an exclusive lock. No other transaction may read or write this row until the exclusive lock is released. This is the key difference from read committed: in read committed, reads don't block writes. In 2PL, a reading transaction holds a shared lock that blocks concurrent writers.

runs.text: 2PL prevents phantoms by using predicate locks (or index-range locks in practice). MySQL InnoDB's serializable level uses 2PL — it locks every row read with a shared lock, ensuring that concurrent modifiers of those rows must wait.
The significant downsides of 2PL:

items.text: Deadlocks

— T1 holds a lock that T2 wants, and T2 holds a lock that T1 wants. The database must detect the cycle and abort one transaction. Deadlock detection adds overhead; applications must be prepared to retry aborted transactions.
Lock contention and reduced throughput

— readers block writers and writers block readers. On a hot row, transactions queue up, and average latency climbs steeply with concurrency. Performance under 2PL can be an order of magnitude worse than under snapshot isolation for read-heavy workloads.
Slow-transaction cascades
— a single slow transaction holding a lock can block many queued transactions, causing latency spikes that look like an outage to the application.

explanation.caption: Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent

runs.text: Two-Phase Locking means: readers lock what they read, writers lock what they write, and nobody releases any lock until the transaction commits. This gives you true serializability, but every read and write is potentially blocked by every other, causing deadlocks and high latency under contention.

cards.title: Serialisable: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)
cards.teaser: SSI, introduced in PostgreSQL 9.1 (2011) and adopted by CockroachDB and Spanner, achieves full serializability using snapshot isolation as a base — optimistically letting transactions run without blocking, then aborting any whose snapshot-read assumptions were violated by a concurrent commit.

runs.text: SSI was introduced by Michael Cahill in his 2008 PhD thesis and implemented in PostgreSQL 9.1. Its core insight: snapshot isolation already prevents most anomalies. The remaining anomalies — write skew and phantoms — follow a specific pattern detectable at commit time. If you track that pattern and abort transactions that exhibit it, you get serializability without blocking reads.
The pattern SSI detects is called a
read-write anti-dependency cycle

. In the doctor on-call example: T1 reads the on-call table (before T2's write), and T2 reads the same table (before T1's write). Both read data that the other will change. When both commit, the database detects that their reads and writes formed a cycle — an outcome that cannot be produced by any serial execution — and aborts one of them.
Implementation in PostgreSQL: the engine tracks two sets of dependencies for each transaction:

items.text: SIREAD locks (predicate locks)

— recorded when a transaction reads a row or a range, noting which data the transaction's decision depended on. Unlike 2PL shared locks, SIREAD locks do not block concurrent writers — they are purely for tracking dependencies.
Outgoing and incoming edges

— when a writer updates a row that another transaction has a SIREAD lock on, an edge is recorded in the dependency graph. The database checks for cycles in this graph at commit time. If a cycle is found, one transaction is aborted.

runs.text: The key advantage over 2PL: SSI transactions never block each other on reads. Reads proceed at snapshot isolation speed. Conflicts are detected and resolved at commit time by aborting one transaction. The abort rate depends on contention — at low concurrency, aborts are rare; at high contention on the same rows, the abort rate rises and applications must retry.

CockroachDB and Spanner both implement SSI-style serializability for global distributed transactions. CockroachDB's implementation adds a twist: rather than always aborting the conflicting transaction, it sometimes
refreshes the snapshot
(re-reads all reads made so far to check they are still valid at a newer timestamp) to allow the transaction to commit at a higher timestamp rather than abort.

SSI is the modern default for new systems that want serializability. PostgreSQL has offered it since 9.1 via SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE. It provides full ACID serializability with significantly better read throughput than 2PL, at the cost of occasional transaction aborts that the application must handle with retries.

SSI is optimistic serializability: let transactions run at full snapshot-isolation speed, track which transactions read data that others subsequently wrote, and abort any transaction whose combined reads and writes form a cycle that no serial execution could produce. Reads never block. Conflicts are caught at commit, not during execution.
